name: Exelon Corporation
employees: 20,571 at December 31, 2025 (FY2025 Form 10-K: ComEd 6,688; PECO 3,169; BGE 3,383; PHI 4,422; balance at Exelon Business Services); 'approximately 20,000' on exeloncorp.com
summary: BOTTOM LINE UP FRONT: Exelon is the corpus's largest wires-only utility — six regulated electric and gas distribution companies (ComEd, PECO, BGE, Pepco, Delmarva Power, Atlantic City Electric) serving about 10.7 million customers in PJM with no owned generation since the 2022 Constellation spin — and the utility that invented the transmission security agreement, the FERC-jurisdictional bilateral contract under which a data center posts collateral, accepts a ramp and pays shortfall and termination charges before ComEd builds its interconnection: six ComEd TSAs are active, backed by more than $1B of letters of credit, and the Q2 2026 call cut the 'high-probability' data-center pipeline from 18 GW to 11 GW (4 GW under signed TSAs plus 7 GW pre-TSA, about 9 GW of it ComEd) inside a refined queue of 36 GW because the company 'weeded out speculative projects'. The instrument is now in court: ComEd cancelled the 1.8 GW PowerHouse Hillwood Joliet TSA on July 24, 2026 over a $1 letter of credit, FERC rejected the cancellation on September 22 and sent the contract question to the Northern District of Illinois. Owning no plants, Exelon buys none of the batteries and turbines its load requires — but it is asking to: Atlantic City Electric filed for a 500 MW / four-hour, roughly $1B utility-owned battery at Pittsgrove with Invenergy in July 2026, BGE and Pepco filed batteries into Maryland's storage solicitations, and Butler's campaign for 'utility-owned generation ... as a cost-effective complement' runs through a $9.6–20B Charles River Associates savings estimate and PJM's third consecutive capacity auction at the price cap, 6.8 GW short. BACKGROUND. Chicago; Pennsylvania corporation; Nasdaq: EXC; 20,571 employees. FY2025 GAAP EPS $2.73 and adjusted operating EPS $2.77 on revenue of $24.3B; 2026 guidance $2.81–$2.91 reaffirmed twice with growth 'near the top end' of 5–7 percent through 2029; a $41.7B 2026–2029 capital plan (from $41.3B in February 2026: −$350M of distribution, −$1.1B of PECO and BGE deferrals, +$1.5B of transmission) growing rate base 7.9 percent a year and transmission rate base about 16 percent, with $12–17B of further transmission opportunity not in the plan; equity need $3.4B through 2029, 37 percent priced. ComEd holds about 4.2 million customers in northern Illinois and an all-time peak near 24,000 MW against more than 28,000 MW of large-load requests; the Mid-Atlantic utilities sit in the PJM zones where residential supply costs rose with the auction. Leadership changes on October 5, 2026 (Kleczynski CFO; Jones to Finance and Strategy), a PECO CEO vacancy since April, and Rodney Oddoye's appointment at Pepco Holdings in September. Collection gap: investors.exeloncorp.com returned HTTP 503 on every attempt, so the Q4 2025, Q1 2026 and Q2 2026 earnings decks — the by-utility pipeline split, the TSA-gigawatt reconciliation between 'about 45 percent of 18 GW' (Q4 2025) and '4 GW' (Q2 2026), the capex split by transmission, distribution and gas — were read only through transcripts, the 8-K mirror and Utility Dive; SEC hosts were blocked and the Q2 2026 10-Q was not read; the six operating companies' websites are single-page applications that return no text, so ComEd's own statement on the PowerHouse cancellation, PECO's large-load compliance filing under the PA PUC's model tariff, the Maryland PC72 rate-schedule terms filed September 1, 2026, the ACE battery's BPU docket text and the Q3 2026 earnings date were not found; the ComEd cancellation filing's FERC docket is recorded two ways (ER26-3257 per tftc.io; ER26-1032 per Construction Review Online) against a confirmed TSA docket of ER26-3104.
ecosystemRole: We assess Exelon as the corpus's wires-only counterparty: the utility that connects the most data-center load in PJM outside Dominion and owns none of the generation or storage that serves it, so the storage and gas sellers in this file do not sell to Exelon today — they sell to the developers who hold its transmission security agreements (PowerHouse, Tract, Equinix, QTS, Aligned, Amazon), to the Illinois Power Agency's Indexed Storage Credit procurements (600 MW awarded September 1, 2026 toward 3,000 MW by 2030, 80 MW of it in the ComEd zone), and to Maryland's Next Generation Energy Act solicitations. Basis: the FY2025 10-K ('The Registrants do not own generation'), the Q2 2026 call's pipeline ladder, the IPA's procurement results and the CRGA's design, in which ComEd runs a virtual power plant rider rather than buying batteries. The exception that would change this is the Atlantic City Electric petition of July 24, 2026 — a 500 MW / four-hour, about $1B ACE-owned rate-based battery at Pittsgrove Township developed, built and operated with Invenergy, with a NJ BPU decision targeted for February 2027 — and behind it the legislative campaign (Maryland's HB 1561 'utility-owned backstop', the CRA report, Butler's 'if the merchant, independent guys won't build, we will' as voiced by Pepco Holdings' Anthony) that would make Exelon a direct buyer of storage and dispatchable capacity for the first time since 2022. For the hyperscalers and developers in the corpus Exelon is the utility whose contract they sign first: the TSA's ramp, readiness, credit, committed-revenue and termination-fee schedule is the template FERC accepted under Mobile-Sierra over the Illinois attorney general's protest, the ICC's Rider DE deposits ($1M at 50 MW, $500,000 per additional 100 MW above 200 MW, a letter of credit above $2M) are the entry fee, and the PowerHouse Joliet dispute is the live test of what happens when a developer reads the credit clause differently from the utility.

productsAndServices.name: ComEd regulated delivery service and the large-load framework — Rider DE / LDPAC deposits (ICC 25-0677/25-0679) and FERC transmission security agreements
productsAndServices.description: Commonwealth Edison delivers electricity to about 4.2 million customers across 11,450 square miles of northern Illinois (70 percent of the state's population) under Illinois's restructured model — ComEd owns wires, not plants; supply comes from the Illinois Power Agency's procurements or retail suppliers — with an all-time system peak of about 24,000 MW and a multi-year rate plan (2024–2027; the ICC approved a $243M reconciliation increase on December 18, 2025, effective January 1, 2026) succeeded by the $15.3B 2028–2031 Multi-Year Integrated Grid Plan filed January 16, 2026 (Docket 26-0047; order expected December 15, 2026), in which data centers are 47 percent of new substation demand. Its large-load framework has two layers. At the ICC, the March 19, 2026 order in consolidated Dockets 25-0677/25-0679 approved revisions to Rider DE (Rider Distribution System Extension) and the General Terms and Conditions for Large Demand Project Applicants or Customers (LDPAC) — any single request for 50 MW or more of new or increased load within ten years: a $1M deposit for 50–200 MW plus $500,000 for each additional 100 MW above 200 MW, a letter of credit from an A3/A- bank when the deposit exceeds $2M, a two-deposit structure (planning and engineering study; long-lead materials), deposits credited to project costs or retained net of ComEd's costs on cancellation, and Rider DE extended to cover additional distribution construction for standard service; ComEd told the commission it had 75-plus applications totalling more than 28,000 MW. The ICC called the order 'an important first step', ordered a staff-initiated investigation within eight months (by April 23, 2026) into whether LDPACs warrant a separate tariff, whether Riders NS and ZSS need modification alongside Rider DE, and how interconnection costs are assigned, and required ComEd workshops and an annual compliance report from February 1, 2027. At FERC, ComEd's Transmission Security Agreements — bilateral contracts for transmission-connected loads filed since December 19, 2025 — carry 'defined ramp, customer facility readiness obligation, credit obligations, committed revenue contributions, shortfall payments if usage misses commitments, and published termination-fee schedule', with collateral in the form of letters of credit guaranteeing transmission revenue for the first ten years of operation. FERC accepted Karis Critical (about 500 MW, ER26-3087) on February 17, 2026 and Equinix (ER26-3101), Grundy County Power NR I — Tract's Morris park (ER26-3100), PowerHouse Hillwood Holding (ER26-3104) and QTS Investment Properties Chicago (ER26-3102) on March 10, 2026, after Aligned Data Centers, Monarch Rock Air (about 1,200 MW) and Red Energy Partners (ER26-841), applying the Mobile-Sierra presumption over the Illinois attorney general's protest that 'the safeguards in the TSA do not prevent existing customers from paying the costs'. ComEd cancelled the PowerHouse Hillwood TSA (and the pending ICC retail agreement) on July 24, 2026 over the timing and form of the security deposit — PowerHouse posted a $1 letter of credit — and FERC rejected the notice of cancellation on September 22, declining primary jurisdiction over 'the interpretation of ambiguous contract terms involving credit support' and leaving the question to the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois (Commissioner LaCerte: '$1 ... an embarrassing legal fiction'). On September 16 ComEd signed two more TSAs with unnamed developers: six active, more than $1B of letters of credit, a queue down from about 39 GW in late 2025 to about 25 GW.

productsAndServices.name: The data-center pipeline — Exelon's ladder from 36 GW of requests to 4 GW under signed TSAs
productsAndServices.description: Exelon reports its large-load book as a ladder whose rungs have changed name as the TSA process matured. At the Q1 2025 call the total was 36 GW with 16 GW 'high probability' (projects in official engineering phases with deposits); Q3 2025 (November 4) put the 'advanced' pipeline at 18 GW with 6 GW 'close to signing TSAs' and 47 GW of potential additions, and PECO signed the first Exelon TSA (Amazon Data Services, Falls Township, Pennsylvania; accepted by FERC November 21, 2025 over PJM's market monitor); the Q4 2025 deck (February 12, 2026) described 'committed data center projects of approximately 18 GW' with 'approximately 45 percent secured with TSAs' and about $1B of collateral; Q1 2026 held 18 GW high-probability and 43 GW under study. On the Q2 2026 call (July 30) the queue was 'refined' from 43 GW to 36 GW: 4 GW under signed TSAs backed by about $1B of collateral, 7 GW 'high probability' that pre-dated the TSA process, and 25 GW under study — so the headline high-probability figure fell from 18 GW to 11 GW ('we have now weeded out speculative projects, and it gives us proactive insight into what is real'), of which about 9 GW is ComEd and about 2 GW the Mid-Atlantic utilities. Jones's timing from 2025 stands: about 10 percent online by 2028, a third by 2030, three-quarters by 2034. The TSA-backed gigawatts fell from roughly 8 GW (45 percent of 18) to 4 GW between the Q4 2025 and Q2 2026 disclosures while collateral stayed at about $1B — the deck that would reconcile the two was not readable — and the PowerHouse cancellation of July 24 is the one named removal. Named projects on the record: PowerHouse Hillwood's Joliet Technology Center (1.8 GW, about $20B, 795 acres, 24 buildings in four phases; annexed 8–1 on March 19, 2026); Tract's Morris Technology Park (about 1 GW; first power June 2028); Equinix at Minooka (700 MW, EEI); QTS Investment Properties Chicago; Karis Critical (about 500 MW); Monarch Rock Air (about 1,200 MW); Aligned; Red Energy Partners; Compass Datacenters' $10B Hoffman Estates campus (Building 1 topped out February 2026; the developer withdrew a rezoning request in July 2026); Stream Data Centers at Elk Grove Village (260 MW; ComEd substation groundbreaking September 2025); CyrusOne's 480 MW Yorkville campus and Aurora site; Prime Data Centers' 270 MW ORD01; Amazon at Falls Township ($20B of planned Pennsylvania data centers, EEI); Pepco Holdings' 34 active projects and 13 GW of potential (March 2026). ComEd's KARE project — a six-mile 345 kV double-circuit line and a 345/138 kV substation south of DeKalb, the first ComEd line to need ICC siting since 2017 — was approved August 24, 2026 without a named customer.

productsAndServices.name: The Mid-Atlantic utilities — PECO, BGE and Pepco Holdings under Pennsylvania's model tariff, Maryland's RELIEF Act, Delaware's GS-LL and New Jersey's A796
productsAndServices.description: PECO (about 1.7 million electric and 553,000 gas customers in southeastern Pennsylvania), BGE (1.4 million electric and 700,000-plus gas customers in central Maryland) and Pepco Holdings — Pepco (1.0 million in DC and Montgomery and Prince George's counties), Delmarva Power (0.6 million electric plus northern Delaware gas) and Atlantic City Electric (0.6 million in southern New Jersey) — are distribution and transmission utilities in PJM's eastern zones, where the 2028/29 Base Residual Auction cleared at the $325/MW-day cap and Exelon says residential supply costs could rise 'up to 80 percent over five years'. Their large-load rules are being written state by state in 2026. Pennsylvania: the PUC's first-of-its-kind large-load model tariff (Docket M-2025-3054271; framework April 30, final order May 13, 2026) covers customers over 50 MW individually or 100 MW in aggregate with 'but for' cost allocation, contributions in aid of construction, six-month studies, deposits and collateral, minimum terms, exit provisions, ramp schedules, a self-build option and a public queue, to be implemented through utility-specific filings — PECO's own filing was not found; the PUC is also opening emergency-curtailment rules (tentative order October 1, 2026) and a ratemaking and ROE working group. PECO's politics dominate: it filed a $429M electric and $81M gas case on March 30, 2026 (ROE 10.95 percent), Governor Shapiro called it 'pure greed', PECO withdrew both on April 16 ('Pennsylvanians are struggling with basic necessities like gas, food, and energy'), CEO David Vahos became a special advisor on April 21 with Innocenzo interim, IBEW Local 614 struck for three days in July, and Barclays, BMO and Mizuho downgraded the stock. Maryland: the Next Generation Energy Act (SB937/HB1035, May 20, 2025) affirmed multi-year plans, barred post-2025 reconciliation filings, set a 150 MW distribution-storage program and expedited-CPCN solicitations for dispatchable generation; the Utility RELIEF Act (HB 1532, passed April 13, signed May 12, effective July 1, 2026) lowered the large-load threshold to 25 MW and load factor to 60 percent, banned forecast test years for a year, ended the 0.5 percent RTO-participation ROE adder (Maryland's agencies filed a FERC complaint on July 2 to strip it from BGE, Delmarva and Pepco — more than $20M a year) and opened Pepco's Phase II cost-removal proceeding; on September 1, 2026 the Maryland Exelon companies filed proposed large-load rate schedules in PC72 (terms not found). Rate outcomes are tightening: the PSC awarded Pepco $50.9M of the $119.9M it asked at a 9.40 percent ROE on August 28, 2026 (Order 92607, Case 9820; $164.9M of White Flint capital disallowed), cut Pepco's reconciliation from $30.6M to $13.4M in March, granted BGE about $77M of a $152M true-up in December 2025, and has BGE's Case 9888 ($156.1M, ROE 10.4 percent, decision January 2027) pending; Maryland's flexible-load plans (Case 9761) are 188 MW at BGE, 185 MW at Pepco and 34 MW at Delmarva. Delaware: the PSC opened Docket 25-0826 on October 15, 2025 and paused interconnections of 25 MW or more until a tariff exists; Delmarva filed GS-LL (General Service – Large Load) for 50 MW or more on December 19, 2025 (workshop February 17; comments March 6, 2026; final order not found); Starwood Digital's 'Project Washington' at Delaware City lost its Coastal Zone appeal and was withdrawn on August 28, 2026; Delmarva's $67.8M base-rate case (25-1555) has interim rates. New Jersey: A796 (passed June 30, 2026; loads of 50 MW or more; financial guarantees of 85 percent of requested service for ten years; BPU authority to use TSAs) awaited the governor's signature; ACE's electric settlement ($54M at 9.60 percent) took effect December 1, 2025. DC: the Court of Appeals reversed the PSC's approval of Pepco's 'Climate Ready Pathway' multiyear plan (April 2026); Order 22860 kept current rates and denied refunds pending remand (Formal Case 1176; evidentiary hearing October 13–14, 2026).

productsAndServices.name: Transmission — $41.7B of 2026–2029 capital, transmission rate base growing 16 percent a year, $12–17B of upside, MISO Tranche 2.1 with Invenergy
productsAndServices.description: Transmission is where Exelon's growth has moved: the FY2025 10-K's $41.3B four-year plan (2026 $9,950M; ComEd $3.5B in 2026 with $1.1B of transmission; PECO $2.225B; BGE $2.175B; PHI $2.05B) was raised to $41.7B at Q1 2026 by adding $1.5B of transmission while cutting $350M of distribution and deferring $1.1B at PECO and BGE, and Butler said 80–100 percent of the capex increases across planning cycles have gone to transmission. Rate base grows about $23B to 2029 (7.9 percent a year), transmission rate base about 16 percent a year, and the company cites $12–17B of identified transmission opportunity over the next decade not in the plan, including PJM's 2025 reliability window ($1.2B recommended to Exelon utilities) and 765 kV work — Khouzami: Exelon is 'one of very few transmission operators that own and operate' 765 kV. In MISO, FERC's August 14, 2026 order approved cost allocation for Tranche 2.1 facilities built in PJM and assigned ComEd about $904M of projects, ComEd bid about $1.9B of Illinois Tranche 2.1 projects with Invenergy, and two more competitive bids (the MARS and EASL projects in Iowa) have results due in the fourth quarter of 2026. Named 2026 work: ComEd's KARE 345 kV line and substation near DeKalb (ICC certificate August 24, 2026), a $590M Champlain substation upgrade (PJM TEAC, September 2025), three new Chicago substations and two in northern Illinois in the 2028–2031 grid plan, and BGE's Key Crossing Reliability Initiative (397-foot monopoles, with Sargent & Lundy). Transmission formula rates for June 2025–May 2026: ComEd +$127M at an 11.50 percent allowed ROE; PECO +$22M (10.35 percent); BGE +$35M, Pepco +$51M, DPL +$23M (10.50 percent); ACE −$57M. Financing: $3.4B of equity through 2029 (about $850M a year, 37 percent priced by Q2 2026 through forwards and the ATM, covering 2026 and half of 2027; $1B of 3.25 percent convertible notes December 2025); 86 percent of 2026 debt done by July (ComEd $1,425M, BGE $925M, Pepco $130M in May–June); operating ROE 9–10 percent; FFO/debt about 14 percent.

productsAndServices.name: Utility-owned storage and the generation campaign — ACE's 500 MW Pittsgrove battery with Invenergy, Maryland's storage solicitations, Illinois's 3 GW procurement, and the PJM argument
productsAndServices.description: Exelon owns no generation and, until July 2026, no utility-scale storage. Atlantic City Electric changed the first half of that on July 24, 2026 by petitioning the New Jersey BPU (Utility Dive cites Docket 2114561) for a 500 MW / four-hour battery on ACE-owned land at Pittsgrove Township, Salem County — an ACE-owned, rate-based asset developed, built and operated with Invenergy at about $1B, in service late 2030, with federal tax credits and PJM capacity and energy revenues offsetting about 70 percent of cost, more than $700M of claimed net customer benefit ($1.36 per $1), no bill impact for the first five years, a 9.6 percent base ROE with performance incentives, and a decision targeted for February 2027 (Butler: 'final order anticipated H1 2027'); no battery supplier is named. In Maryland, the PSC's Order 92281 (Case 9715, April 8, 2026) set the Next Generation Energy Act's 150 MW distribution-storage program — BGE proposed 29 MW (3 MW BGE-owned, 15 MW customer-sited, 11 MW third-party) and PHI 14.5 MW of third-party front-of-meter batteries (Pepco 10.5 MW, Delmarva 4.0 MW) — and BGE and Pepco submitted projects to the state's transmission-connected storage solicitation (megawatts and docket not found); the Round 2 expedited-CPCN solicitation for dispatchable generation (ELCC 65 percent or more) and 'large capacity energy resources' of 20 MW or more runs October 1–31, 2026 (PC 74) for third-party developers. In Illinois, the Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act (Public Act 104-0458, signed January 8, 2026) set a 3,000 MW storage target by 2030 procured by the Illinois Power Agency through Indexed Storage Credits — the first procurement (August 26, 2026) awarded 600 MW of a 1,038 MW target, 520 MW in MISO and 80 MW in the ComEd zone, approved September 1 — and ComEd's role is the Rider SDVPP virtual power plant (effective July 16, 2026; about 1.8 GW of connected DER) and a 25 percent larger efficiency budget, not ownership. The campaign: Charles River Associates' February 2026 report for Exelon estimates utility-generated power could save PJM customers $9.6–20.0B in 2028/29 and cut supply-caused unserved energy 85 percent; Butler supports Maryland's HB 1561 'utility-owned backstop, particularly storage and renewable resources', calls the Pennsylvania generation bill 'a long shot', and told the Q2 call that 'utility-owned generation needs to be part of that mechanism as a cost-effective complement to market-based solutions' after PJM's third consecutive auction at the cap ($325/MW-day; 6,831 MW short; 525 MW of new generation; a simulated uncapped price of about $555 RTO-wide and $777 in ComEd). Exelon's 2024 petition at FERC against Constellation's nuclear co-location deals, and its protest with AEP of the Talen–Amazon Susquehanna agreement, are its documented positions on behind-the-meter supply.

strategyRead: (High confidence) We assess that the transmission security agreement is now the standard instrument for connecting a data center in ComEd's territory and that the PowerHouse dispute will narrow, not end, it: FERC left the TSA in force and sent only the credit-clause question to court, ComEd signed two more TSAs seven weeks after the cancellation, and New Jersey's A796 and Maryland's PC72 filings are copying the form. Basis: the September 22, 2026 FERC order and the LaCerte and Rosner concurrences pressing for clearer security-deposit rules; Daily Energy Insider's September 16 account (six active TSAs, more than $1B of letters of credit); the ICC's parallel LDPAC investigation. We expect the next generation of TSAs to specify the collateral instrument and timing explicitly, which is the fix the $1 letter of credit exposed.

(High confidence) We assess that Exelon's 4 GW of TSA-backed load is the most bankable data-center number in the corpus and its 25 GW 'under study' the least, and that the company will keep cutting the middle rung rather than growing it. Basis: Jones's 'we have now weeded out speculative projects', the fall from 18 GW to 11 GW between Q1 and Q2 2026, the queue's contraction from about 39 GW to about 25 GW at ComEd, and the ~36-month interconnection cycle against a 2028 first-tranche date. The unreconciled gap — TSA gigawatts falling from about 8 GW to 4 GW while collateral held at about $1B — is the number to test at the Q3 call.

(High confidence) We assess that Exelon is not a buyer of storage or generation equipment in 2026 and that its route to becoming one runs through state legislatures, with New Jersey's decision on the ACE Pittsgrove battery (about February 2027) the first real test. Basis: the 10-K ('The Registrants do not own generation'); the CRGA design that routes Illinois's 3 GW through the IPA and gives ComEd a VPP rider; Maryland's NGEA program (3 MW BGE-owned); the ACE petition's 9.6 percent-plus-incentives ROE ask and $1.36-per-$1 benefit claim; Butler's 'utility-owned generation ... as a cost-effective complement' and Anthony's 'we will'. If Pittsgrove is approved, Invenergy — not Exelon — selects the battery, as at We Energies' build-transfer projects.

(Moderate confidence) We assess that the Mid-Atlantic utilities will carry more regulatory risk than growth through 2027 and that the ComEd share of the high-probability book will rise above its current ~80 percent. Basis: the RELIEF Act's 25 MW threshold and RTO-adder repeal, the Pepco order's 9.40 percent ROE and $164.9M disallowance, the PECO withdrawal and CEO change, Delaware's interconnection pause and the collapse of the Delaware City project, against ComEd's transmission ROE of 11.50 percent, its $904M of Tranche 2.1 allocations and six TSAs. The Q1 2026 reallocation — $1.1B deferred at PECO and BGE, $1.5B added to transmission — is the company already acting on this read.

(Moderate confidence) We assess that PJM's capacity price, not Exelon's own rates, is the political variable that decides whether the generation campaign succeeds, and that a fourth auction at the cap in December 2026 would move Maryland's HB 1561 or its successor. Basis: three consecutive auctions at the collar with 6.8 GW of shortfall and 525 MW of new supply; the company's own simulation of $555–777/MW-day uncapped; the ACE bill-impact figures; the CRA report's $9.6–20B; consumer advocates' August 2026 request that FERC reject PJM's reliability backstop. Pennsylvania remains 'a long shot' by the CEO's own description.

(Low confidence) We assess that the Constellation re-merger speculation of 2025 has no live basis: no first- or third-party source in the record reports talks, Constellation's 2025–2026 M&A was Calpine, and the two companies are adversaries at FERC over nuclear co-location. Basis: absence of evidence across the newsroom sitemap, RTO Insider and Utility Dive searches; the 2024 declaratory-order petition. policyExposure.exposure: The 2028/29 Base Residual Auction cleared every zone at the $325/MW-day UCAP cap — the third consecutive auction at the FERC-approved collar — 6,831 MW short of the reliability requirement, with the requirement up 1,374.5 MW 'largely due to additional Large Loads' and only 524.7 MW of new generation and uprates; Exelon's own simulation puts the uncapped price at about $555 RTO-wide and $777 in ComEd. Exelon's customers pay it through supply charges (ACE residential +$14.70–23.64 a month if the cap lifts; Mid-Atlantic supply costs 'up to 80 percent over five years'), and the company's response is political: utility-owned generation 'as a cost-effective complement', the CRA report ($9.6–20B of savings), support for the collar's extension (April 2026) and PJM's reliability backstop, and Maryland's HB 1561. Consumer advocates asked FERC in August 2026 to reject the backstop.
policyExposure.mitigation: Collar extension; TSAs that assign transmission cost and collateral to large loads; the ACE battery and Maryland storage petitions as owned capacity; demand response (ComEd 1,105.6 MW cleared).

policyExposure.regime: FERC — transmission security agreements, large-load show-cause orders and co-location
policyExposure.exposure: ComEd's TSAs are FERC contracts under the Mobile-Sierra presumption, so their disputes go to FERC and federal court: the September 22, 2026 order rejecting ComEd's PowerHouse cancellation declined jurisdiction over 'ambiguous contract terms involving credit support', with Rosner and LaCerte pressing for clearer security-deposit rules and Chang's March concurrence warning that bilateral agreements 'may not be sufficient to ensure that customers are protected against unjust cost shifts'. FERC's June 18, 2026 show-cause orders require PJM and five other RTOs to address large-load interconnection (>50 MW at >69 kV), cost transparency, co-location and flexible service by mid-November 2026; PJM's co-location package (effective June 1, 2029) is protested by Vistra, Constellation and the Data Center Coalition; Exelon's 2024 petition against Constellation's nuclear co-location and its Susquehanna protest with AEP are its documented positions. Maryland's July 2, 2026 complaint seeks to strip the 0.5 percent RTO adder from BGE, Delmarva and Pepco (>$20M a year).
policyExposure.mitigation: Six active TSAs with LOCs covering ten years of transmission revenue; explicit collateral terms in the next TSAs; ComEd's 11.50 percent transmission ROE; the ICC's parallel LDPAC investigation as the state backstop.

policyExposure.regime: Illinois — CRGA (Public Act 104-0458), the ICC large-load order and the stalled POWER Act
policyExposure.exposure: The Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act (signed January 8, 2026; provisions effective from June 2026) sets 3,000 MW of storage by 2030 procured by the IPA through Indexed Storage Credits (600 MW awarded September 1, 2026), a statewide IRP (first filing November 15, 2026), utility virtual power plants (ComEd's Rider SDVPP, effective July 16, 2026) and 25 percent larger efficiency budgets — with no utility-owned generation authority. The ICC's March 19, 2026 order approved ComEd's Rider DE and LDPAC deposits 'as an important first step' and opened an eight-month investigation into a separate large-load tariff, Riders NS/ZSS and cost allocation; ComEd must report annually from February 1, 2027. The POWER Act (HB 5513: a separate data-center rate class, self-supply with renewables and storage, water reporting, community benefit agreements) stalled in committee in May 2026; Governor Pritzker suspended data-center tax credits in June and is pressing the October veto session; CUB estimates $24–37B of statewide cost. ComEd's $15.3B 2028–2031 grid plan awaits a December 15, 2026 order.
policyExposure.mitigation: TSAs and LDPAC deposits as the cost-shift defense; Rider SDVPP; the $243M 2026 reconciliation already approved; the $60M Customer Relief Fund.

policyExposure.regime: Maryland — Next Generation Energy Act (2025) and Utility RELIEF Act (HB 1532, 2026)
policyExposure.exposure: The NGEA (May 20, 2025) affirmed multi-year plans, barred post-2025 reconciliation filings, created the 150 MW distribution-storage program (Order 92281: BGE 29 MW, PHI 14.5 MW), dispatchable-generation and transmission-connected storage solicitations (PC 74 Round 2 open October 1–31, 2026) and Legislative Energy Relief Refunds (BGE $49M, Pepco $21M, DPL $8M twice). The RELIEF Act (passed April 13, signed May 12, effective July 1, 2026) lowered the large-load threshold to 25 MW and the load factor to 60 percent, banned forecast test years for a year, barred MYRP true-ups, ended the RTO adder and opened Pepco's Phase II cost-removal proceeding; the Maryland Exelon companies filed PC72 large-load rate schedules on September 1, 2026. The PSC's August 28 Pepco order (42 percent of the ask at a 9.40 percent ROE; $164.9M disallowed) and the December 2025 BGE true-up (about $77M of $152M) show the ratemaking climate; HB 1561's utility-owned-generation authority remained pending in the sources read.
policyExposure.mitigation: Single-year cases (BGE 9888); the flexible-load plans (Case 9761; 407 MW across BGE, Pepco and Delmarva); BGE and Pepco battery bids into the state solicitations.

policyExposure.regime: Pennsylvania, Delaware and New Jersey large-load rules; affordability politics
policyExposure.exposure: Pennsylvania's PUC model large-load tariff (M-2025-3054271, May 13, 2026) is voluntary and awaits PECO's utility-specific filing (not found); the PUC's curtailment rulemaking (tentative order October 1, 2026; final target January 28, 2027), cost-allocation conference and ROE working group follow PECO's withdrawn $510M request and Governor Shapiro's 'pure greed'. Delaware paused interconnections of 25 MW or more (October 15, 2025) pending Delmarva's GS-LL tariff (≥50 MW; final order not found) and enacted a data-center clean-power law in August 2026 (terms not accessible); New Jersey's A796 (≥50 MW; 85 percent / ten-year guarantees; TSAs) awaited signature after passing June 30, 2026. DC's Court of Appeals reversed the PSC's approval of Pepco's multiyear plan (April 2026), with current rates kept pending remand.
policyExposure.mitigation: Generation investment 'as a last resort' and capital decisions 'informed by customer affordability considerations' (PECO/Exelon, April 2026); $1.1B of PECO and BGE deferrals; the shift of capital to FERC-regulated transmission.

policyExposure.exposure: Exelon's federal tax exposure runs through the customers' bills rather than its own plants: Treasury's February 2026 Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax notice is worth up to $200M of customer savings over four years by the company's estimate, and the ACE Pittsgrove battery's economics assume 'early-year federal tax credits' and PJM revenues offset about 70 percent of its roughly $1B cost — the project's key federal dependency after the OBBBA's accelerated phase-outs. No FEOC or battery-tariff statement was found (Butler, April 2025: tariffs about 1.5 percent of capex and O&M, 'manageable'); the battery's supplier is unnamed and the IPA's Indexed Storage Credit procurements carry sourcing risk with the developers.
policyExposure.mitigation: Rate-based recovery with a 9.6 percent-plus ROE ask on Pittsgrove; Invenergy as developer; state procurements that leave equipment risk with third parties.
